list_secrets.title: List the secrets in the vault
list_secrets.description:
Every secret in the vault by name, with its enabled state, content type, expiry, tags and timestamps -- but NOT its value. That makes this the safe inventory call: it answers "what is in this vault" and "which secrets are about to expire" without any secret material crossing the wire.
Page with the `nextLink` the response carries.

max_results.description: How many secrets per page, up to 25.

output.description: The vault's secrets, without their values.

items.description: id, contentType, attributes (enabled, created, updated, exp, nbf) and tags.

get_secret.title: Read a secret's value
get_secret.description:
Return a secret's plaintext value. This is a credential leaving the vault: do not log the response, include it in a summary, or send it anywhere the secret is not meant to go.
Omitting `version` reads the current version, which is what you almost always want -- pinning to a version means a rotation will not reach you. A disabled or expired secret returns 403 rather than its value.
get_secret.notes: Returns the secret in plain text. Handle the response as a credential.

version.description: A specific version id. Leave as the default empty value to read the current version, which is normally what you want.

output.description: The secret and its value. Secret.

contentType.description: What the value is, if the writer said.

attributes.description: enabled, created, updated, exp and nbf.

set_secret.title: Create a secret or add a new version
set_secret.description:
Store a value under a name. If the name already exists this creates a NEW VERSION rather than overwriting -- the old version stays readable by its own id, which is what makes rotation safe and also means a secret written by mistake is still there until purged.
`expires` and `not_before` are Unix timestamps. Setting an expiry does not delete the secret; it makes get_secret refuse to return it after that point, which is usually what you want for a credential with a known lifetime.
set_secret.notes: Creates a new version rather than replacing. Old versions remain readable by id.

secret_name.description: The secret's name. Letters, digits and hyphens.

content_type.description: A hint about what the value is, e.g. "password" or "application/json".

tags.description: Tags for the secret, as a flat map.

enabled.description: Whether the new version can be read. Defaults to true.

expires.description: Expiry as a Unix timestamp. get_secret refuses the value after it.

not_before.description: Unix timestamp before which the secret cannot be read.

output.description: The secret as stored, including its value.

attributes.description: enabled, created, updated, exp and nbf.

update_secret_attributes.title: Enable, disable or re-date a secret
update_secret_attributes.description:
Change a secret's metadata without changing its value -- disable it, set or clear an expiry, adjust its tags or content type.
Disabling is the reversible half of revocation: get_secret starts refusing immediately, and enabling it again restores access. That is usually the right first move during an incident, before deciding whether to delete.

version.description: The version to change. Leave empty for the current version.

enabled.description: False makes get_secret refuse the value; true restores it.

expires.description: New expiry as a Unix timestamp.

not_before.description: New not-before time as a Unix timestamp.

tags.description: Tags to store on the secret.

output.description: The secret's metadata after the change; no value is returned.

attributes.description: The updated enabled, exp and nbf.

list_secret_versions.title: List a secret's versions
list_secret_versions.description: Every version of one secret, with each version's enabled state and timestamps but not its value. This is the rotation history: it shows when the secret last changed, and gives the version ids that get_secret can pin to if an old value is needed.

max_results.description: How many versions per page, up to 25.

items.description: id (including the version), attributes and tags.

delete_secret.title: Delete a secret
delete_secret.description:
Delete a secret and all its versions. On a soft-delete vault -- which is every vault by default -- the secret moves to a deleted state rather than disappearing: list_deleted_secrets shows it and recover_deleted_secret brings it back, for the vault's retention period.
The name stays reserved while the secret is soft-deleted, so creating a new secret with the same name fails until it is recovered or purged.
delete_secret.notes: Soft-deleted, not destroyed. The name stays reserved until the secret is recovered or purged.

output.description: The deleted secret, with its recovery id and scheduled purge date.

recoveryId.description: The id under which it can be recovered.

scheduledPurgeDate.description: When it will be purged automatically, as a Unix timestamp.

list_deleted_secrets.title: List soft-deleted secrets
list_deleted_secrets.description: Secrets that have been deleted but are still recoverable, with their deletion date and scheduled purge date. The first call after "someone deleted the secret", and also the explanation for a set_secret that fails with a name conflict on a name nothing seems to be using.

max_results.description: How many entries per page, up to 25.

items.description: id, recoveryId, deletedDate, scheduledPurgeDate and attributes.

recover_deleted_secret.title: Recover a soft-deleted secret
recover_deleted_secret.description: Bring a deleted secret back, with all its versions and its original name. Works for as long as the secret appears in list_deleted_secrets. Recovery is asynchronous but usually quick.

secret_name.description: The deleted secret's name, from list_deleted_secrets.

purge_deleted_secret.title: Permanently destroy a soft-deleted secret
purge_deleted_secret.description:
Destroy a soft-deleted secret immediately and irrecoverably, before its scheduled purge date. There is no undo and no backup unless one was taken with backup_secret first.
Fails with 403 on a vault with purge protection enabled -- that setting exists precisely to make this impossible, and it cannot be turned off once on.
purge_deleted_secret.notes: Irreversible. Blocked entirely on vaults with purge protection enabled.

secret_name.description: The deleted secret to destroy permanently.

backup_secret.title: Back up a secret
backup_secret.description:
Export an encrypted blob containing every version of a secret. The blob can only be restored into a vault in the same Azure subscription and geography, and it is opaque -- but it is still derived from secret material, so store it as one.
The reason to use it is that restore_secret is the only way to move a secret between vaults with its version history intact, and the only recovery path once a secret is purged.
backup_secret.notes: The blob is restorable secret material. Store it as a credential.

value.description: Base64url-encoded backup blob; pass it to restore_secret.

restore_secret.title: Restore a secret from a backup
restore_secret.description:
Recreate a secret, with all its versions, from a backup_secret blob. Only works into a vault in the same subscription and geography as the one it came from.
Fails if a secret with that name already exists in the target vault -- restore cannot merge into or overwrite an existing secret.
restore_secret.notes: Fails if the secret name is already in use in the target vault.

list_keys.title: List the keys in the vault
list_keys.description: Every key in the vault, with its type, enabled state and timestamps. Private key material never appears -- keys exist to be used inside the vault, not read out of it, which is the whole reason to store something as a key rather than as a secret.

max_results.description: How many keys per page, up to 25.

items.description: kid (the key id), attributes (enabled, created, updated, exp) and tags.

get_key.title: Get a key's public part and metadata
get_key.description: A key's public material, type, allowed operations and attributes. The private half never leaves the vault -- to actually use the key, call sign_with_key, verify_with_key, encrypt_with_key, decrypt_with_key, wrap_key or unwrap_key, all of which run inside the HSM.

version.description: A specific version. Leave empty for the current one.

output.description: The key's public JWK and metadata.

key.description: The public JWK -- kid, kty, key_ops and the public parameters.

attributes.description: enabled, created, updated, exp and recoveryLevel.

create_key.title: Create a key in the vault
create_key.description:
Generate a new key inside the vault. The private material is created there and can never be exported, which is the security property that makes this different from storing a PEM as a secret.
`RSA` with 2048 or 4096 bits, or `EC` with a named curve, are the usual choices; the `-HSM` variants are backed by a hardware module and are only available on a Premium vault. `key_ops` narrows what the key may be used for -- a signing key that cannot decrypt is a smaller blast radius.
Creating a key under an existing name adds a version rather than replacing.

key_type.description: RSA or EC for a software-protected key; the -HSM variants need a Premium vault. oct-HSM is for symmetric keys on Managed HSM.

key_size.description: RSA key size in bits. Ignored for EC keys.

curve.description: Elliptic curve name, for EC keys.

key_operations.description: What the key may do -- sign, verify, encrypt, decrypt, wrapKey, unwrapKey. Narrow it to what is actually needed.

enabled.description: Whether the key can be used. Defaults to true.

output.description: The new key's public part and metadata.

key.description: The public JWK, including the versioned kid.

sign_with_key.title: Sign a digest with a vault key
sign_with_key.description:
Produce a signature using a key that never leaves the vault. The `value` is the DIGEST of the data, base64url-encoded -- not the data itself -- and it has to match the algorithm's hash size (32 bytes for RS256 and ES256, 64 for RS512). Hashing is the caller's job; the vault only signs.
The principal needs a crypto role such as Key Vault Crypto User.
sign_with_key.notes: Takes the base64url-encoded digest, not the raw data. The caller hashes first.

algorithm.description: Signature algorithm. Must match the key type and the digest length.

digest.description: The base64url-encoded hash of the data to sign, of the length the algorithm requires.

version.description: A specific key version. Leave empty for the current one.

kid.description: The exact key version that signed.

verify_with_key.title: Verify a signature with a vault key
verify_with_key.description:
Check a signature against a digest using a vault key. Only necessary when the key's public part is not available to the caller -- for a normal public key, verifying locally is free and does not spend a vault operation.
As with signing, `digest` is the hash, base64url-encoded, not the data.

algorithm.description: The algorithm the signature was made with.

digest.description: The base64url-encoded hash that was signed.

version.description: A specific key version. Leave empty for the current one.

value.description: True when the signature checks out.

wrap_key.title: Wrap a symmetric key with a vault key
wrap_key.description:
Encrypt a small piece of key material -- typically a data-encryption key -- with a key held in the vault. This is envelope encryption: the data key encrypts the bulk data locally, and only the wrapped data key needs storing, because unwrap_key is the only way to get it back.
The input is limited to roughly the key's block size, so this is for keys, not for data.
wrap_key.notes: For key material only. RSA wrapping is limited to a few hundred bytes.

algorithm.description: Wrapping algorithm. RSA-OAEP-256 is the current recommendation.

key_material.description: The base64url-encoded key material to wrap.

version.description: A specific key version. Leave empty for the current one.

kid.description: The key version that wrapped it -- unwrapping needs the same one.

unwrap_key.title: Unwrap a key with a vault key
unwrap_key.description:
Decrypt key material that wrap_key produced, returning the original data key in plain text. The response is key material: treat it as a credential.
Must be unwrapped with the same key VERSION that wrapped it -- the `kid` the wrap response returned. A rotation does not break old wrapped keys, but only because the old version is still there.
unwrap_key.notes: Returns plaintext key material. Handle the response as a credential.

algorithm.description: The algorithm the key was wrapped with.

wrapped_key.description: The base64url-encoded wrapped key from wrap_key.

version.description: The key version that wrapped it, from the wrap response's kid. Leave empty only if the key has never been rotated.

delete_key.title: Delete a key
delete_key.description: Delete a key and all its versions. Soft-deleted on a normal vault, so it is recoverable for the retention period -- but anything encrypted or wrapped with it becomes undecryptable the moment it goes, and stays that way if it is ever purged. Check what depends on the key before deleting.
delete_key.notes: Anything encrypted or wrapped with the key cannot be recovered once the key is purged.

output.description: The deleted key, with its recovery id and scheduled purge date.

recoveryId.description: The id it can be recovered under.

list_certificates.title: List the certificates in the vault
list_certificates.description: Every certificate in the vault, with its thumbprint, enabled state and -- the field that matters -- `attributes.exp`, the expiry as a Unix timestamp. This is the call for an expiry sweep: it needs no permission to read private material and covers the whole vault in one page or two.

max_results.description: How many certificates per page, up to 25.

include_pending.description: Include certificates whose issuance is still in progress.

items.description: id, x5t (thumbprint), attributes (enabled, created, exp, nbf) and tags.

get_certificate.title: Get a certificate
get_certificate.description: One certificate's public part: the DER-encoded certificate in `cer`, its thumbprint, its policy, and the ids of the key and secret that hold its private material. The private key itself is behind those -- readable only by a principal with secret permissions, which is a distinction worth remembering when handing out access.

version.description: A specific version. Leave empty for the current one.

output.description: The certificate's public material and policy.

kid.description: Id of the key holding the private half.

sid.description: Id of the secret holding the full PFX or PEM.

policy.description: Issuer, key properties, lifetime actions and the subject.

get_certificate_policy.title: Get a certificate's issuance policy
get_certificate_policy.description: How a certificate is issued and renewed: the issuer, the key type and size, the subject and SANs, and the `lifetimeActions` that decide when auto-renewal fires. A certificate that expired despite "auto-renew being on" is explained here -- usually a Self issuer, or a renewal trigger set later than the issuer's own lead time.

issuer.description: The issuer name -- Self, Unknown, or a configured CA.

x509_props.description: subject, sans, key usage and validity_months.

lifetime_actions.description: When renewal or email is triggered.

delete_certificate.title: Delete a certificate
delete_certificate.description: Delete a certificate along with the key and secret behind it. Soft-deleted on a normal vault, so recoverable for the retention period. Anything serving TLS from this certificate keeps working until it next reloads it, which makes the breakage look delayed.

output.description: The deleted certificate, with its recovery id.

recoveryId.description: The id it can be recovered under.
